A.tagline: See AI's arrival as inevitable, and are the least convinced it's already doing harm.
A.description: Compared to other participants, people in this group are far more likely to see AI's arrival as inevitable, something to adapt to rather than resist or slow down, and they are the least persuaded that AI is already causing real harm, from spreading misinformation to displacing artists and writers. They're also the most open to AI-driven economic development, including data centers, and the least convinced its environmental costs outweigh the benefits.

B.tagline: Agree that AI already delivers real benefits, but want real accountability from AI companies.
B.description: This is the largest group, and its members' stance is conditional: they agree AI already delivers real benefits and isn't going away, but unlike Optimists, they take long-term risks to humanity seriously and want real accountability from AI companies, opposing liability shields and tax breaks that aren't tied to responsible use. They reject both the idea that AI is eroding human cognition and the claim that its costs outweigh its benefits.

C.tagline: The most doubtful that AI's benefits are worth its environmental and human cost.
C.description: Compared to other participants, people in this group are the most doubtful that AI's benefits are worth its costs, especially its environmental footprint and its effect on human creativity and thinking, and the most convinced its gains are concentrated among a small number of companies rather than the broader economy. They're the least persuaded that change is simply inevitable, or that AI tools, education, or university partnerships are actually helping ordinary people.
